title: Building Scalable REST APIs with Spring Boot: A Practical Guide
tags: Java · Spring Boot · REST APIs · Backend
content:
Building a REST API is one of the most common responsibilities of a Java backend engineer. However, writing an endpoint that works locally is only the beginning. A production-ready API must also consider validation, error handling, security, performance, maintainability, and observability.

Spring Boot simplifies application development by providing auto-configuration, starter dependencies, embedded servers, and a consistent programming model. These features allow developers to focus on business logic rather than spending excessive time configuring infrastructure.

In this article, we will build a mental model of a well-structured REST API and explore practical techniques that make backend services easier to test, maintain, and scale.

## 1. Start with a Clear Layered Architecture

A common Spring Boot application separates responsibilities into controller, service, and repository layers. Each layer has a specific purpose, which reduces coupling and makes the code easier to understand.

The controller handles HTTP requests and responses. It should validate request structure, delegate business operations, and return suitable status codes. It should not contain complex business rules or direct database queries.

The service layer implements business use cases. It coordinates repository operations, applies business rules, and defines transaction boundaries where appropriate. Keeping this logic outside controllers makes it reusable across multiple entry points.

The repository layer manages data access. Spring Data JPA can generate common database operations automatically, while custom queries handle more specialized requirements.

For example, a typical request follows this path: Client → Controller → Service → Repository → Database. The response then travels back through the same application layers.

## 2. Design Meaningful API Endpoints

Good endpoint design makes an API predictable. Prefer resource-oriented paths such as GET /api/orders, GET /api/orders/42, POST /api/orders, and DELETE /api/orders/42.

Use HTTP methods according to their intended semantics. GET retrieves a resource, POST creates a resource or initiates an operation, PUT replaces a resource, PATCH partially updates a resource, and DELETE removes a resource when supported by the business rules.

Status codes should communicate the result clearly. Use 200 OK for successful requests that return a response, 201 Created when a resource is created, 204 No Content when a successful response has no body, 400 Bad Request for invalid input, 401 Unauthorized for missing or invalid authentication, 403 Forbidden for insufficient permissions, 404 Not Found for a missing resource, and 500 Internal Server Error for unexpected failures.

Avoid returning HTTP 200 for every outcome. Clients should not need to inspect an arbitrary message to determine whether an operation succeeded.

## 3. Use DTOs Instead of Exposing Entities

A database entity represents persistence concerns, while a Data Transfer Object represents the data exchanged through an API. These models serve different purposes and should not automatically be treated as interchangeable.

Exposing entities directly can reveal internal fields, create accidental coupling between the database schema and public API, and cause serialization problems when entities contain relationships. DTOs allow the API contract to evolve independently from persistence details.

For example, a CreateOrderRequest might contain customerId and items, while an OrderResponse might contain orderId, status, totalAmount, and createdAt. The internal entity can include additional database fields that clients do not need to know about.

DTOs also provide a natural place to define request validation rules. Bean Validation annotations such as @NotBlank, @NotNull, @Positive, and @Size can express constraints directly on request models.

## 4. Validate Requests at the Boundary

Validation should happen as close as possible to the incoming request. Reject invalid data before it reaches the business layer or database.

For example, a transfer request should require a positive amount, a valid destination account, and all mandatory fields. Structural validation can be handled with Bean Validation, while business validation belongs in the service layer.

There is an important distinction between checking whether an amount is positive and checking whether an account has sufficient funds. The first is a basic input constraint; the second depends on business state and must be evaluated as part of the operation.

Do not rely exclusively on frontend validation. API clients can include web applications, mobile applications, scheduled jobs, and external integrations. The backend must enforce its own rules.

## 5. Centralize Exception Handling

Scattered try-catch blocks make API behavior inconsistent. Spring provides @RestControllerAdvice and @ExceptionHandler to centralize exception-to-response mapping.

A useful error response contains a stable error code, a human-readable message, a timestamp, and relevant validation details. Avoid returning stack traces, database credentials, SQL statements, or internal implementation details to clients.

For example, an invalid request might return an error code such as VALIDATION_ERROR and a list of fields that failed validation. A missing order might return ORDER_NOT_FOUND.

Stable error codes are particularly useful when multiple frontend applications or external services consume the same API. The display message can change without forcing clients to parse arbitrary text.

## 6. Manage Database Transactions Carefully

The @Transactional annotation allows Spring to manage a transaction around a method. It is commonly used when a business operation requires multiple database changes to succeed or fail together.

Consider an order workflow that creates an order and its order items. If saving an item fails after the order has been inserted, the application should not leave behind an incomplete order. A transaction can provide atomicity for the participating database operations.

Transactions do not automatically make a distributed workflow atomic across databases, Kafka, external APIs, and file systems. These systems require additional design considerations, such as the transactional outbox pattern, idempotent consumers, or a saga where appropriate.

Keep transaction boundaries focused. Long-running transactions can hold locks, increase contention, and reduce throughput. Avoid performing slow network calls inside a database transaction unless the design explicitly accounts for the consequences.

## 7. Add Security from the Beginning

Authentication answers the question, 'Who are you?' Authorization answers, 'What are you allowed to do?' A secure API needs both.

Spring Security can authenticate users through session-based mechanisms, OAuth 2.0, or JWT-based approaches, depending on the application architecture. A valid token does not automatically mean that the caller can access every resource.

For example, a user may have permission to view orders but not to approve refunds. Authorization should enforce both role-level permissions and relevant resource-level access rules.

Never store plaintext passwords. Use an appropriate password-hashing mechanism when managing credentials, protect secrets outside source control, validate tokens correctly, and require HTTPS in production.

Security also includes input handling, least-privilege database accounts, safe logging, dependency updates, and careful management of sensitive information in API responses.

## 8. Improve Performance with Evidence

Performance optimization should begin with measurement rather than assumptions. Start by examining request latency, database query duration, connection-pool utilization, memory usage, and error rates.

Database indexes can improve query performance when they match common access patterns, but unnecessary indexes increase storage costs and make writes more expensive. Examine query plans and realistic data volumes before deciding which indexes to add.

Pagination is usually preferable to returning thousands of records in a single response. A paginated endpoint allows clients to retrieve manageable result sets and reduces unnecessary memory consumption.

Caching can help when data is expensive to retrieve and does not change too frequently. Redis is one option for distributed caching, but cache invalidation, expiration, consistency, and failure behavior must be considered.

Connection pools, appropriate timeouts, and efficient database access are also important. Adding more application instances will not solve every bottleneck, especially when all instances compete for a constrained database.

## 9. Write Tests That Protect Behavior

Unit tests should cover business rules without requiring a real database or running application server. Mockito can isolate dependencies, while JUnit provides the test structure and assertions.

Controller tests can verify request validation, status codes, and response structures. Integration tests can verify that the application interacts correctly with its database, security configuration, and other infrastructure.

A useful test suite covers successful scenarios, invalid input, missing resources, permission failures, and unexpected dependency behavior. Boundary cases are especially important for financial calculations and state transitions.

Avoid tests that merely repeat the implementation line by line. Prefer tests that express observable behavior, because those tests are more likely to remain valuable when internal code changes.

## 10. Make APIs Observable

Production debugging is difficult when logs contain only generic messages. Structured logs with correlation identifiers can help engineers trace a request across multiple services.

Metrics such as request count, latency percentiles, error rate, and active requests help identify trends before users report a problem. Distributed tracing can reveal where time is spent across service boundaries.

Logs should provide useful operational context without exposing passwords, access tokens, personal information, or confidential business data. Define retention and access policies for production telemetry.

## Final Thoughts

A reliable REST API is the result of several small engineering decisions working together. Clear layer boundaries, DTOs, validation, consistent errors, transaction management, security, testing, and observability all contribute to maintainability.

You do not need to introduce every possible framework or architectural pattern into a small application. Start with the simplest design that satisfies the requirements, measure actual problems, and add complexity only when it provides a clear benefit.

The most useful question is not whether an API uses the latest technology. It is whether the API behaves predictably, protects its data, handles failures responsibly, and remains understandable as the application grows.

title: Understanding Kafka Through an Order Processing System
tags: Apache Kafka · Java · Event-Driven Architecture · Microservices
content:
As applications grow, a single synchronous request can become responsible for too many operations. An order service might need to save an order, reserve inventory, initiate payment, send a notification, and update analytics. If every operation must finish before the request returns, overall latency and availability can suffer.

Event-driven architecture offers another approach. A service publishes an event describing something that happened, and other services consume that event when they are ready. Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform commonly used to support these workflows.

## 1. Understand Events

An event records a fact that has already occurred. OrderCreated, PaymentCompleted, and InventoryReserved are examples. An event is different from a command, which asks a component to perform an action.

A command might say ReserveInventory. An event might say InventoryReserved. Naming events in the past tense helps communicate that the event represents a completed fact rather than an instruction.

Events should contain the information consumers need to process them. A typical OrderCreated event might include an eventId, orderId, customerId, totalAmount, and occurredAt timestamp. The exact fields depend on the domain and the data-sharing requirements.

## 2. Learn the Core Kafka Concepts

A producer publishes records to a Kafka topic. A topic is a named stream of records, such as orders or payments. Topics are divided into partitions, which provide a way to distribute data and processing across a cluster.

Each record in a partition receives an offset. The offset identifies its position within that partition. Kafka preserves record order within a partition, but there is no single global ordering guarantee across all partitions of a topic.

A broker is a Kafka server. A cluster contains multiple brokers that collectively store and serve topic partitions. Replication can improve availability by keeping copies of partitions on multiple brokers.

A consumer reads records from Kafka. Consumers can work independently or join a consumer group. Within a consumer group, a partition is assigned to at most one consumer at a time, allowing work to be distributed across the group.

## 3. Choose Message Keys Carefully

The record key influences partition selection. If events for the same order use orderId as the key, they can be routed to the same partition under a consistent partitioning strategy.

This is useful when the application needs per-order ordering. For example, OrderCreated should logically precede OrderCancelled for the same order. Using a stable key helps preserve the ordering of those records within their partition.

However, a single very busy key can create a hot partition. Partition-key design should reflect ordering requirements, throughput, and how evenly traffic is distributed.

## 4. Think About Delivery Semantics

Distributed systems can fail between processing a message and recording that processing has completed. A consumer might update the database successfully and then crash before committing its Kafka offset. After restarting, it may receive the same event again.

This is why consumers should be designed for duplicate delivery. Idempotent processing means that processing the same event repeatedly has the same intended effect as processing it once.

For example, a consumer can maintain a processed_events table with a unique event identifier. Within a database transaction, it checks whether the event has already been processed, applies the business update if necessary, and records the event identifier.

Kafka supports different delivery and transaction capabilities, but end-to-end exactly-once business behavior is not automatically guaranteed across arbitrary databases and external systems. The application must design for the actual failure boundaries involved.

## 5. Handle Failures Intentionally

A consumer can fail because of temporary database unavailability, malformed data, network timeouts, or business validation errors. Retrying every error indefinitely can block progress and overload dependencies.

Use bounded retries with backoff for transient errors. Permanent failures should be handled differently. Depending on the system, an invalid message may be sent to a dead-letter topic for inspection and later reprocessing.

A dead-letter topic is not a substitute for monitoring. Track retry counts, consumer lag, failure rates, and the age of the oldest unprocessed record. Alerting helps the team identify problems before the backlog becomes critical.

## 6. Understand Consumer Lag

Consumer lag represents how far behind a consumer group is relative to the latest available records. A growing lag may indicate insufficient consumer capacity, slow downstream operations, uneven partition traffic, or a sudden increase in event volume.

Adding consumers can improve throughput only when there are enough partitions to distribute across them. If a topic has four partitions, one consumer group cannot actively assign those four partitions to more than four consumers at the same time.

Scaling should be based on measurements. Increasing consumer count without examining database capacity can simply move the bottleneck downstream.

## 7. Consider the Transactional Outbox Pattern

A common reliability problem occurs when a service updates a database and publishes a Kafka event as two separate actions. The database transaction may succeed while publishing fails, leaving other services unaware of the change.

The transactional outbox pattern addresses this by saving the business update and an event record in the same database transaction. A separate publisher reads the outbox and sends events to Kafka. The publisher can retry delivery when Kafka is unavailable.

Because a publisher may send an event more than once, consumers should still be idempotent. The pattern improves consistency between committed database state and event publication, but it does not eliminate the need for retry and monitoring strategies.

## 8. Test the Failure Scenarios

A useful event-driven system should be tested beyond the happy path. What happens if Kafka is unavailable when an application starts? What happens if the consumer processes a duplicate event? What happens when the database is unavailable for several minutes?

Test event serialization, schema compatibility, consumer group behavior, retries, duplicate handling, and recovery after restarts. Integration tests using a real Kafka environment or an appropriate test setup can reveal problems that isolated unit tests miss.

## Final Thoughts

Kafka is not simply a faster way to call another service. It changes the relationship between services by introducing durable event streams, asynchronous processing, partition-based ordering, and independent consumer progress.

The strongest implementations begin with clear event contracts and explicit failure handling. Once those fundamentals are in place, partitioning, replication, consumer scaling, and operational monitoring can be designed around measurable requirements.

title: Redis Caching: Benefits, Trade-Offs, and Common Mistakes
content:
Caching is one of the most familiar performance techniques in backend development. Instead of repeatedly retrieving the same data from a slower source, an application stores a reusable copy in a faster layer.

Redis is an in-memory data store that supports strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, and other data structures. It is often used for caching, counters, rate limiting, temporary state, and coordination use cases.

Caching can reduce database load and improve response times, but it introduces consistency and operational trade-offs. A cache should solve a measured problem rather than become an additional dependency without a clear purpose.

## 1. The Cache-Aside Pattern

In the cache-aside pattern, the application checks the cache before querying the primary data source. If the item exists, the application returns the cached value. If it does not exist, the application loads the data from the database, stores a copy in the cache, and returns the result.

The application controls cache population and invalidation. This makes cache-aside relatively straightforward to introduce into an existing Spring Boot service.

For example, a product details endpoint might use a key such as product:123. When the product is requested repeatedly, Redis can serve the response without executing the same database query each time.

## 2. Choose Cache Keys Deliberately

Cache keys should be predictable, consistent, and specific enough to identify the cached representation. A key such as customer:42:profile communicates its purpose more clearly than a vague key such as data42.

If the cached result depends on tenant, locale, permissions, or query parameters, those dimensions may need to be reflected in the key. Otherwise, the application could accidentally return data generated for a different request context.

Avoid putting secrets or unnecessary personal information into keys. Keys may appear in operational tools, metrics, logs, and debugging output.

## 3. Set Expiration Policies

A time-to-live determines how long a cached item remains available before expiration. Shorter expiration reduces the time stale data can remain in the cache but may increase database traffic. Longer expiration can improve hit rates while increasing the potential for stale responses.

The right TTL depends on the data. Public reference data may tolerate a longer TTL than account balances or frequently changing inventory.

Expiration is not the only invalidation strategy. When an update occurs, the application may explicitly remove or refresh the corresponding key. This can reduce staleness but requires reliable invalidation logic across every relevant update path.

## 4. Understand Cache Invalidation

Cache invalidation becomes difficult when multiple services can modify the same underlying data. One service may update the database while another continues serving an older cached copy.

Possible strategies include time-based expiration, explicit eviction after writes, event-driven invalidation, and versioned cache keys. Each approach has trade-offs involving complexity, freshness, and failure recovery.

For example, if a database update succeeds but cache eviction fails, the application may temporarily serve stale data. The design should define whether that inconsistency is acceptable and how it is eventually corrected.

## 5. Prevent Cache Stampedes

A cache stampede occurs when many requests simultaneously miss the same key and all attempt to load the same expensive data from the database.

Possible mitigations include request coalescing, short-lived locks where appropriate, prewarming frequently accessed keys, and adding random variation to expiration times. The best solution depends on how expensive the load operation is and how much coordination the system can tolerate.

Do not introduce distributed locking automatically. Locks add failure modes and should be used only when simpler approaches are insufficient.

## 6. Plan for Redis Unavailability

A cache is an optimization only if the application can safely handle its failure. Some applications can bypass Redis and read from the database, while others use a controlled fallback or temporarily reject requests to protect an already overloaded dependency.

If every cache failure sends all traffic to the database, the database may become overwhelmed. Timeouts, concurrency limits, circuit breakers, and sensible fallback policies can reduce the risk of a cascading failure.

The correct fallback depends on the business operation. Serving slightly stale public metadata may be acceptable, while silently returning stale financial information may not be.

## 7. Monitor Cache Effectiveness

Track cache hit rate, miss rate, memory usage, eviction activity, latency, connection errors, and key expiration patterns. A high hit rate is useful only when the cache actually reduces total cost without violating correctness requirements.

If a key is almost never reused, caching it may add overhead without meaningful benefit. If the cache consumes too much memory, eviction policies may remove valuable entries and lower the hit rate.

## Final Thoughts

Redis can be a valuable component in a Spring Boot architecture, but it is not a replacement for database design or query optimization. Start by identifying expensive, frequently repeated reads, define acceptable staleness, choose an invalidation policy, and measure the outcome.

A well-designed cache makes the application faster without making its correctness impossible to reason about.

title: What I Learned from Debugging Production Issues
content:
Production incidents are uncomfortable, especially when users are waiting for a business-critical workflow to complete. They are also opportunities to understand how an application behaves under conditions that development environments rarely reproduce perfectly.

A good incident response focuses first on limiting impact, then on identifying the cause, and finally on preventing recurrence. Blame does not restore service or improve system reliability.

## 1. Establish What Changed

When an issue appears, begin with facts. Identify the affected service, approximate start time, impacted users, failed operation, and whether the problem affects every request or only a subset.

Review recent deployments, configuration changes, dependency failures, traffic increases, and infrastructure events. A recent change is a useful lead, but it is not proof of causation.

Compare successful and unsuccessful requests. Differences in payload size, user permissions, data state, or downstream dependencies can reveal patterns that are not obvious from a single error message.

## 2. Read Logs with Context

A stack trace tells you where an exception occurred, but it may not fully explain why the operation failed. Correlate the exception with the request, relevant business identifiers, downstream calls, and preceding log events.

Correlation IDs make it easier to follow one request through multiple services. Structured logs can make filtering and aggregation much more reliable than searching free-form messages manually.

Avoid logging sensitive data simply to make debugging easier. Access tokens, passwords, and confidential customer information should not appear in ordinary application logs.

## 3. Separate Symptoms from Root Causes

A timeout in an API gateway may be a symptom rather than the original failure. The actual cause could be a slow SQL query, exhausted connection pool, stalled downstream service, lock contention, or a retry storm.

Similarly, a high error rate might originate from a dependency rather than from the application code itself. Trace the request path and verify each assumption with evidence.

A root-cause analysis should explain the failure mechanism, not merely repeat the final exception message. Saying 'the API failed because of a timeout' describes the symptom; explaining why the operation exceeded its deadline is more useful.

## 4. Recover Safely

During an incident, the fastest action is not always the safest action. Restarting a service may temporarily restore functionality, but it can also erase useful process state or cause in-flight work to be retried.

Before retrying a failed operation, understand whether it is idempotent. Retrying a read is generally different from retrying a payment, a journal submission, or another operation that creates durable business effects.

When possible, use bounded retries, clear timeouts, idempotency keys, and explicit job states. These controls make recovery more predictable when a dependency becomes unavailable and then recovers.

## 5. Write a Useful Post-Incident Review

A useful review records the impact, timeline, detection method, root cause, resolution, and follow-up actions. It should distinguish confirmed facts from hypotheses and document what evidence supported the conclusion.

Follow-up actions should be specific and verifiable. Examples include adding an alert for a growing queue, introducing a missing database index after query-plan analysis, improving timeout configuration, or adding a regression test for a previously unhandled edge case.

Avoid action items such as 'be more careful' or 'monitor better'. They are difficult to measure and do not change the system in a reliable way.

## 6. Improve the System After Recovery

The end of the incident is not the end of the work. Review whether the same failure could affect other services, whether alerts were triggered early enough, and whether recovery steps were documented clearly.

Runbooks should explain how to recognize common failure patterns, which dashboards to inspect, which actions are safe, and when to escalate. They should also be updated when the architecture changes.

## Final Thoughts

Production support develops engineering judgment. It teaches you to reason about incomplete information, distinguish symptoms from causes, and balance rapid recovery against data correctness.

The long-term goal is not to eliminate every failure. It is to build systems that detect problems quickly, limit their impact, recover safely, and become more resilient through what the team learns.

title: A Practical Guide to Writing Better Unit Tests in Java
content:
Tests are most valuable when they give developers confidence to change code without breaking important behavior. A test suite that passes consistently can make refactoring safer, expose edge cases, and document the intended behavior of a component.

In Java applications, JUnit 5 is commonly used to organize and execute tests, while Mockito helps isolate the class being tested from its dependencies. These tools work best when the tests have clear responsibilities and meaningful assertions.

## 1. Test Behavior, Not Private Implementation

A unit test should describe what a component promises to do. For an order service, this may mean creating an order when the request is valid, rejecting an invalid amount, or reporting that a requested product does not exist.

Tests that depend heavily on private method names or internal call sequences can break during harmless refactoring. Verify externally meaningful results and interactions that are part of the component's contract.

## 2. Follow Arrange, Act, Assert

Arrange the required inputs and dependencies. Act by invoking the method under test. Assert that the observed result matches the expected behavior.

A clear structure makes tests easier to scan. Each test should have one primary reason to fail, and its name should explain the scenario being verified.

For example, a test named createOrder_rejectsNegativeAmount describes both the operation and the expected behavior. It is more informative than a generic name such as testOrder2.

## 3. Use Mockito to Isolate Dependencies

Suppose an OrderService depends on an OrderRepository. A unit test can mock the repository so that it controls the returned data and verifies the service's behavior without connecting to a real database.

Mocks are useful for dependencies whose behavior must be controlled, such as external services or repositories. However, excessive mocking can make a test mirror the implementation rather than verify meaningful behavior.

If a test becomes complicated because it needs many mocks, the class may have too many responsibilities or an overly complicated dependency structure.

## 4. Cover Failure Paths

Happy-path tests are necessary, but they do not demonstrate how a service behaves when something goes wrong. Test missing data, invalid input, permission failures, and dependency exceptions where those cases are relevant.

For financial or inventory operations, also test boundary conditions such as zero values, repeated requests, concurrent updates, and unexpected state transitions. The right cases depend on the business rules rather than on a fixed checklist.

## 5. Understand Unit and Integration Tests

Unit tests isolate a small piece of logic. Integration tests verify that multiple components work together, such as a Spring repository interacting with a real database or a controller working with security configuration.

Neither type replaces the other. Unit tests are generally faster and more focused, while integration tests catch issues involving configuration, serialization, database behavior, and framework integration.

A balanced test suite uses each level for the problems it is best suited to detect.

## 6. Keep Tests Deterministic

A deterministic test produces the same result under the same conditions. Tests that depend on the current time, random values, shared state, or external services can become unreliable if those dependencies are not controlled.

Use fixed test data, isolate resources, and clean up persistent state where necessary. Avoid relying on the execution order of tests unless the framework and test design explicitly require it.

## Final Thoughts

Strong tests are not measured only by line coverage. They are measured by how effectively they detect meaningful regressions and how clearly they communicate expected behavior.

Start with important business rules, add tests for known failure modes, and keep the suite readable. A small collection of precise tests is often more useful than a large collection of assertions that do not protect real requirements.
